interview_metadata.name: Jacob Bowden
interview_metadata.protocol: American Voices Project (Park et al. 2024, Table 7) — Full 109 questions

transcript.question_text: To start, I would like to begin with a big question: tell me the story of your life. Start from the beginning -- from your childhood, to education, to family and relationships, and to any major life events you may have had.
transcript.response: I was born in Torrance and pretty much raised around the South Bay, mostly Redondo and Hawthorne when I was little. My dad worked with his hands, mostly maintenance and construction jobs, and my mom worked at a grocery store deli counter. We were not rich, but we had a roof, food, and a lot of rules about pulling your weight. School was never my strong suit. I made it through eighth grade, started ninth, and then I drifted out because I was already working odd jobs and thought money in my pocket mattered more than sitting in class. Looking back, I wish I had finished, but back then nobody could tell me much. I got into painting through an older guy named Ray who let me scrape trim and clean brushes on apartment jobs. I found out I had a good eye for color and prep work, and over time that became my trade. I married Linda in my late twenties, and we had two kids, Sarah and Daniel. The marriage was good for a while, then work stress, money stress, and me being gone too much wore it down. We divorced about twelve years ago. These days I live alone in North Redondo, still paint houses and commercial spaces, surf when the water is decent, fish when I can, and I am trying to move from just being the guy on the ladder to having a small green-paint contracting outfit with a couple younger apprentices.

follow_ups.question: When you think about childhood, what scene comes back first?
follow_ups.response: Probably Saturday mornings, my dad loading tools in the truck and me tagging along half-asleep with a donut in my hand. I remember the smell of sawdust, primer, and coffee.

follow_ups.question: Who taught you the most about painting?
follow_ups.response: Ray Martinez taught me the basics. He was strict about sanding and taping. He used to say the paint job is mostly what nobody sees underneath.

transcript.question_text: Some people tell us that they've reached a crossroads at some points in their life where multiple paths were available, and their choice then made a significant difference in defining who they are. What about you? Was there a moment like that for you, and if so, could you tell me the whole story about that from start to finish?
transcript.response: The big one was leaving school. I was fourteen, fifteen, acting older than I was, and I had a choice between sticking it out or going full-time into work. My parents argued about it. My mom wanted me back in school, my dad figured a trade could keep me out of worse trouble. I picked work, and it shaped everything after that. It gave me pride and a way to earn, but it also boxed me in later because licenses, paperwork, bids, and business stuff all ask for things I never finished. Now I am circling back, looking at GED classes and the contractor license, because I do not want the next chapter blocked by a decision I made as a kid.

follow_ups.question: What did you feel at the time?
follow_ups.response: Mostly free, honestly. I liked getting paid cash and being treated like a worker. The regret came later.

follow_ups.question: What would you tell your younger self?
follow_ups.response: I would tell him to keep the job but finish school at night. Pride does not pay every bill.

transcript.question_text: Some people tell us they made a conscious choice or decision in moments like these, while others say it 'just happened'. What about you?
transcript.response: It felt like it just happened, but really I made choices every week. I stopped going one day, then two days, then I was working more than studying.

follow_ups.question: Did anyone try to pull you back?
follow_ups.response: My mom did. A school counselor called once or twice, but I avoided it.

follow_ups.question: Do you still think about that?
follow_ups.response: Yes, especially when I fill out forms or study license books and feel behind.

transcript.question_text: Do you think another person or an organization could have lent a helping hand during moments like this?
transcript.response: Yes. If there had been a real trade-school path where I could work and still finish credits, I might have stayed connected. I needed structure, not a lecture.

follow_ups.question: What kind of structure would have helped?
follow_ups.response: Morning classes, afternoon job site, and somebody checking if I showed up.

follow_ups.question: Did you ever find that kind of support later?
follow_ups.response: Mostly through older tradesmen. They taught me work habits, but not school habits.

transcript.question_text: Moving to present time, tell me more about family who are important to you. Do you have a partner, or children?
transcript.response: I am divorced and not living with a partner. My ex-wife Linda and I are civil now. We do not hang out, but we can talk about the kids without a fight. My daughter Sarah is thirty-one and lives in Long Beach. She works in a dental office and has a little boy, Mateo, who is six. My son Daniel is twenty-eight, lives in San Pedro, and works around boat repair and marina maintenance. I see Sarah maybe twice a month and Daniel about once a month unless we meet for a Dodgers game or he needs help with something. My older sister Karen is in Torrance, and she is the one who keeps family birthdays from falling apart. Family matters to me, even if I am not the guy calling every day.

follow_ups.question: What do you usually do when you see your grandson?
follow_ups.response: We go to the beach path, get tacos, or I let him help water the succulents. He likes looking at my old car posters.

follow_ups.question: Who do you call first if something serious happens?
follow_ups.response: Probably Karen, then Sarah. Karen is steady and knows how to handle people.

transcript.question_text: Are there anyone else in your immediate family whom you have not mentioned? Who are they, and what is your relationship with them like?
transcript.response: My parents have both passed. I have a younger brother, Mark, in Riverside. We talk a few times a year and get along better with distance.

follow_ups.question: Do you visit Mark?
follow_ups.response: Maybe once a year, usually around a barbecue or somebody's birthday.

follow_ups.question: What were your parents like later in life?
follow_ups.response: My mom stayed warm and worried. My dad got quieter, but he and I made peace.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about anyone else in your life we haven't discussed (like friends or romantic partners). Are there people outside of your family who are important to you?
transcript.response: I have a small crew of friends, mostly from work, surfing, and fishing. My closest friend is Pete Alvarez, another painter who does drywall repair too. We grab coffee at 6 a.m. sometimes before jobs. On weekends in summer I surf with a loose club of older guys at Redondo, and there is a woman named Marcy I have gone to dinner with a few times, but I would not call it serious. I also know people through volunteer painting projects at community centers and churches.

follow_ups.question: How often do you see Pete?
follow_ups.response: At least once a week, sometimes every day if we are on the same job.

follow_ups.question: Where do you and friends usually meet?
follow_ups.response: Coffee shops, the pier, a job site, or somebody's driveway when we are working on a car.

transcript.question_text: Now let's talk about your current neighborhood. Tell me all about the neighborhood and area in which you are living now.
transcript.response: I live in North Redondo, in a small rented one-bedroom back unit behind an older house. It is not fancy beach-front Redondo, more working people, families, contractors, nurses, restaurant folks. You hear leaf blowers, delivery trucks, kids, and sometimes someone running a saw in the garage. I like that I can drive to the beach quick, get to Home Depot, hit job sites in Torrance or Manhattan Beach, and still feel like I know some neighbors. The rents are high, though, and a lot of older places are getting torn down for bigger townhomes.

follow_ups.question: Who do you know nearby?
follow_ups.response: My landlord lives in the front house, and I know the couple next door well enough to bring their trash cans in.

follow_ups.question: What places are part of your routine?
follow_ups.response: The beach, the paint store, Home Depot, a taco place on Artesia, and the community center.

transcript.question_text: Some people say they feel really safe in their neighborhoods, others not so much. How about for you?
transcript.response: I feel pretty safe. I lock my truck because tools get stolen, but walking around at night does not scare me.

follow_ups.question: Have you had tools stolen?
follow_ups.response: Yes, years back somebody took a sander and cords from my truck bed. Since then everything gets locked.

follow_ups.question: Do neighbors look out for each other?
follow_ups.response: A little. People text if a garage door is open or a strange van sits too long.

transcript.question_text: Living any place has its ups and downs. Tell me about what it's been like for you living here.
transcript.response: The upside is the ocean, the weather, and steady work. The downside is cost. A working guy can make decent money and still feel squeezed here.

follow_ups.question: What keeps you from moving cheaper inland?
follow_ups.response: My family, my clients, and the water. Inland heat would make me miserable.

follow_ups.question: What has changed most?
follow_ups.response: More expensive houses and more traffic. The old casual beach town feel is thinner.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about the people who live with you right now, even people who are staying here temporarily.
transcript.response: It is just me in the unit. One bedroom, small kitchen, little patio where I keep succulents and a grill. My grandson might spend an afternoon there, but nobody sleeps there regularly. I like the quiet because after job sites and traffic, I need space to reset.

follow_ups.question: What is your home like day to day?
follow_ups.response: Pretty simple. Work boots by the door, guitar by the couch, paint sample fans on a shelf.

follow_ups.question: Do you prefer living alone?
follow_ups.response: Mostly, yes. Sometimes it gets too quiet, but I like making my own schedule.

transcript.question_text: Is anyone in your household a temporary member, or is everyone a permanent member of the household?
transcript.response: No temporary members. It is only me.

follow_ups.question: Any regular overnight guests?
follow_ups.response: No, not regular.

follow_ups.question: Has that changed recently?
follow_ups.response: No, it has been this way for years.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about anyone else who stays here from time to time, if there is anyone like that
transcript.response: Nobody really stays over. Family visits, then goes home.

follow_ups.question: Who visits most often?
follow_ups.response: Sarah and Mateo, usually on a weekend afternoon.

follow_ups.question: Do friends come by?
follow_ups.response: Pete might stop by to look at a tool or car part.

transcript.question_text: Is there anyone who usually lives here but is away -- traveling, at school, or in a hospital?
transcript.response: No. Nobody else usually lives here.

follow_ups.question: No one away temporarily?
follow_ups.response: No.

follow_ups.question: No students attached to the household?
follow_ups.response: No, my kids are grown and on their own.

transcript.question_text: Right now, across a typical week, how do your days vary?
transcript.response: Monday through Friday I am usually up around 5:15, coffee, check the surf report even if I am working, then I load tools by 6:15. Jobs usually run 7 to 3:30 or 4, depending on light and client rules. Evenings are errands, cleaning brushes, making calls, or studying contractor license material. Saturday depends on work. If I have a deadline, I work half a day; if not, I surf, fish, or see family. Sunday I try to keep slower with laundry, groceries, grilling, and maybe guitar.

follow_ups.question: What is your most predictable day?
follow_ups.response: Monday. I like to start early, set up plastic and drop cloths, and make the week feel organized.

follow_ups.question: When do you usually see friends?
follow_ups.response: Saturday mornings for surf or coffee, and sometimes a Dodgers or Lakers game on TV at Pete's place.

transcript.question_text: At what kind of job or jobs do you work, and when do you work?
transcript.response: I am a painting worker, mostly residential repainting with some small commercial interiors. I do prep, patching, sanding, masking, priming, brush and roller, spray when the site allows it, and color matching. I work for myself on smaller jobs and subcontract under a couple general contractors on bigger ones. Most work is weekday daylight hours, but commercial jobs sometimes happen evenings or weekends if the business needs to stay open.

follow_ups.question: What part of the job do you take most pride in?
follow_ups.response: Prep and clean lines. Anyone can slap paint on, but a good finish starts with patience.

follow_ups.question: Do you manage other workers?
follow_ups.response: Sometimes one or two helpers. I show them setup, safety, and how not to waste material.

transcript.question_text: Do you have other routines or responsibilities that you did not already share?
transcript.response: I check on my sister Karen once or twice a week by phone, and I help my daughter if she needs a repair or Mateo pickup in a pinch. I water my succulents every few days, keep the truck organized, and try to keep Sundays for bills and planning. I also volunteer a few times a year painting community spaces, usually when somebody from church or the center calls.

follow_ups.question: What bills or planning do you do Sunday?
follow_ups.response: Rent reminders, material receipts, tax envelopes, job estimates, and checking what needs to be paid.

follow_ups.question: How do you track work?
follow_ups.response: Mostly a notebook and phone calendar. I am not fancy, but I write everything down.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about any recent changes to your daily routine.
transcript.response: The main change is I have been studying at night for the contractor license and looking into GED prep. That cuts into TV and guitar time. I also started using a phone app for color matching and estimates, which is new for me. My body is making me stretch more in the morning too, because my knees and shoulder complain if I jump straight onto a ladder.

follow_ups.question: How often do you study?
follow_ups.response: Three nights a week if I am honest, about an hour each time.

follow_ups.question: What is hardest about that change?
follow_ups.response: Sitting still after a long day and not feeling embarrassed by what I forgot from school.

transcript.question_text: If you have children, tell me about a typical weekday during the school year for your children. What is their daily routine? And what are after school activities your children participate in?
transcript.response: My children are adults, so I do not have school-year routines for them now. My grandson Mateo is in school, but he lives with my daughter, not me. From what Sarah tells me, he goes to school in Long Beach, then sometimes after-school care or soccer. I help only once in a while if her schedule gets tight.

follow_ups.question: Do you ever do school pickup?
follow_ups.response: Rarely, maybe a few times a year if Sarah is stuck at work.

follow_ups.question: What do you do with Mateo after pickup?
follow_ups.response: Snack, beach walk if there is time, or he watches cartoons while I make dinner.

transcript.question_text: Some people we've talked to tell us about experiences with law enforcement. How about for you?
transcript.response: Mostly traffic stops and job-site stuff. I have been pulled over for an expired registration sticker and once for a brake light on my work truck. Police have come around job sites when neighbors complained about parking or noise. I try to be respectful and keep paperwork straight because a truck full of tools already gets attention.

follow_ups.question: Were those encounters tense?
follow_ups.response: Not really for me, more annoying than scary.

follow_ups.question: Did they change how you act?
follow_ups.response: I keep my registration current and do not leave tools looking suspicious in the open.

transcript.question_text: What other experiences with law enforcement stand out in your mind?
transcript.response: When my tools were stolen, I filed a police report. They were polite, but nothing came back. That taught me insurance and prevention matter more than expecting recovery.

follow_ups.question: Did that cost you work?
follow_ups.response: A little. I had to borrow a sander and replace cords fast.

follow_ups.question: How did you feel about the response?
follow_ups.response: I understood they had bigger cases, but it still felt like working people are on their own.

transcript.question_text: Some people tell us about experiences of arrest -- of loved ones, family members, friends, or themselves. How about for you?
transcript.response: I was never arrested. My younger brother Mark had a DUI years ago, maybe fifteen years back, and that shook the family. He handled the court stuff and has been better since.

follow_ups.question: Did that affect your relationship?
follow_ups.response: For a while, yes. I was mad because he could have hurt somebody.

follow_ups.question: Any friends with arrest experiences?
follow_ups.response: A few old job-site guys had trouble, but nobody close right now.

transcript.question_text: Some people say they vote in every election, some tell us they don't vote at all. How about you?
transcript.response: I vote in presidential elections and most local ones, but I have missed primaries. Mail ballots made it easier. I pay attention more when something affects housing, small business, the environment, or workers. I am not the guy watching politics all day, but I do not like sitting out completely.

follow_ups.question: Do you vote by mail or in person?
follow_ups.response: Mostly by mail now. I fill it out at the kitchen table.

follow_ups.question: Do you discuss voting with family?
follow_ups.response: A little with Sarah and Karen. Daniel tunes it out unless it affects work.

transcript.question_text: How would you describe your political views?
transcript.response: I call myself independent, leaning Democrat most years. I grew up around working people, so I care about wages, health care, and whether a regular person can afford rent. I also run my own work, so I understand small-business complaints about permits, taxes, and regulations getting too tangled. Environment matters to me because I live by the ocean and use paints and solvents, and I have seen the trade move toward low-VOC products for good reason. I am not big on culture-war shouting. I want streets safe, schools decent, and government to do the basics without wasting money. On immigration, I have worked beside a lot of Mexican and Central American tradesmen, and most are just trying to feed family. I do not like people being used as political punching bags.

follow_ups.question: What issues would most affect your vote?
follow_ups.response: Housing costs, health care, environmental rules that make sense, and support for apprenticeships or trade training.

follow_ups.question: Do you trust either party?
follow_ups.response: Not fully. Democrats line up with me more, but both parties talk better than they deliver.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about any recent changes in your political views.
transcript.response: I have gotten more serious about climate and housing. Years ago I thought environmental rules were mostly extra paperwork. Now I see some of them protect workers and neighborhoods, especially with old lead paint and fumes. On housing, I used to think people just needed to work harder, but I know plenty of hard workers who cannot afford a decent place near their jobs. I am still practical, but less quick to blame the person struggling.

follow_ups.question: What changed your mind on housing?
follow_ups.response: Watching rents jump while wages did not keep up, and seeing my own kids priced out of places I used to afford.

follow_ups.question: What changed your mind on environmental rules?
follow_ups.response: Using better coatings and seeing fewer headaches and less smell on indoor jobs.

transcript.question_text: One topic a lot of people have been talking about recently is race and/or racism and policing. Some tell us issues raised by the Black Lives Matter movement have affected them a lot, some say they've affected them somewhat, others say they haven't affected them at all. How about for you?
transcript.response: It affected me somewhat. I am a white guy, and I have not had the same police fear other people talk about. But I have worked with Black and Latino guys who tell different stories, and I believe them. The videos were hard to watch. I did not become an activist, but it made me listen more before giving an opinion.

follow_ups.question: Who did you talk with about it?
follow_ups.response: Mostly coworkers and my daughter. Sarah is more vocal about it than I am.

follow_ups.question: Did it change your view of police?
follow_ups.response: It made me think training and accountability matter more than I used to admit.

transcript.question_text: How have you been thinking about the issues Black Lives Matter raises?
transcript.response: I think the core point is that people want to be treated fairly and not be scared during a traffic stop. I can support that without thinking every officer is bad. My view is practical: if there are patterns where people get treated rougher because of race, fix the pattern. Better training, body cameras, consequences when someone abuses power, and more mental-health response where police are not the only tool.

follow_ups.question: Do people around you agree?
follow_ups.response: Mixed. Some older trades guys get defensive. Younger people seem more open.

follow_ups.question: What would you want local leaders to do?
follow_ups.response: Be honest with numbers and complaints, not just slogans.

transcript.question_text: How have you been thinking about race in the U.S. recently?
transcript.response: I think the country is more mixed than when I was a kid, and that is normal here in Southern California. At the same time, old problems did not disappear. In construction and trades, I have seen who gets hired, who gets paid late, who gets talked down to. I try to judge people by work and character, but I also know systems can favor some people before anyone says a word.

follow_ups.question: Has working in diverse crews shaped that?
follow_ups.response: Yes. Job sites teach you quick that skill comes in every accent and background.

follow_ups.question: Do you think about your own race much?
follow_ups.response: More than before, but not every day. I know being white probably made some situations easier.

transcript.question_text: How have you responded to the increased focus on race and/or racism and policing? Some people tell us they're aware of the issue but keep their thoughts to themselves, others say they've talked to family and friends, others have joined protests. What about you?
transcript.response: I talked with family and coworkers, but I did not join protests. I mostly listened, read some local coverage, and tried not to repeat lazy comments.

follow_ups.question: Did you post online about it?
follow_ups.response: No. I do not use social media for arguments.

follow_ups.question: Did any conversation stick with you?
follow_ups.response: A Latino coworker telling me he teaches his son exactly how to move during a stop. That stayed with me.

transcript.question_text: What about people you're close to? How have they responded to the increased focus on race and/or racism and policing?
transcript.response: Sarah supports the movement more openly and posts about it sometimes. Daniel is quieter but thinks police should be accountable. My sister Karen is moderate and worries about protests turning rough, but she agrees racism is real. Some work friends complain it went too far. I am usually the one saying, 'Just listen before you decide.'

follow_ups.question: Has it caused conflict?
follow_ups.response: A few tense conversations, especially with older coworkers.

follow_ups.question: Do you avoid the topic now?
follow_ups.response: Sometimes. I pick my moment because job sites need to keep moving.

transcript.question_text: Now we'd like to learn more about your health. First, tell me all about your health.
transcript.response: For fifty-eight, I am doing okay but I feel the mileage. My knees ache from ladders, my right shoulder gets stiff from rolling ceilings, and my lower back needs stretching. I do not have diabetes or anything like that as far as I know. I try to surf, walk, and keep my weight reasonable. I eat better when I cook fish and vegetables, worse when I am tired and grab burgers.

follow_ups.question: Do you have a regular doctor?
follow_ups.response: Yes, through a clinic plan, but I do not go as often as I should.

follow_ups.question: What do you do for pain?
follow_ups.response: Stretching, ice, ibuprofen when needed, and trying not to carry everything in one trip.

transcript.question_text: For you, what makes it easy or hard to stay healthy?
transcript.response: Easy is living near the beach because walking and surfing do not feel like exercise. Hard is the job. Painting beats up joints, and after a ten-hour day I do not want a salad and a gym. Money matters too. Dental work, physical therapy, all that can wait too long when cash is tight.

follow_ups.question: What healthy habit sticks best?
follow_ups.response: Morning stretching and beach walks.

follow_ups.question: What habit slips first?
follow_ups.response: Eating right. I will buy gas-station snacks if I am rushing.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about anything big that has happened in the past two years related to your health: any medical diagnoses, flare-ups of chronic conditions, broken bones, pain -- anything like that.
transcript.response: No big diagnosis, but my shoulder flared up last year after a commercial ceiling job. It was a lot of overhead rolling, and I ignored it until I could barely sleep on that side. The doctor called it tendinitis and told me to rest, ice it, and do exercises. I did some, not enough. It still talks to me when I overdo it.

follow_ups.question: Did you miss work?
follow_ups.response: I missed two full days and turned down one small weekend job.

follow_ups.question: Did you get physical therapy?
follow_ups.response: No formal therapy. I got printed exercises and watched a couple videos.

transcript.question_text: Sometimes, health problems get in the way. They can even affect people's ability to work or care for their children. How about you?
transcript.response: They get in the way mostly by slowing me down. I can still work, but I have to be smarter with ladders and overhead work. If my body goes, my income goes.

follow_ups.question: Have you changed how you work?
follow_ups.response: Yes, I use extensions, take breaks, and ask helpers to carry heavier buckets.

follow_ups.question: Does that worry you?
follow_ups.response: Yes. That is part of why I want to move into contracting and mentoring.

transcript.question_text: Sometimes, it's not your health problem, but the health of a loved one. Has this been an issue for you?
transcript.response: My sister Karen had a breast cancer scare a few years ago, but it was caught early and she is doing well. My mom had heart problems before she passed, and that was hard because she needed rides and help understanding appointments. Right now nobody immediate is in crisis, but at my age you know that can change fast.

follow_ups.question: Do you help Karen now?
follow_ups.response: Mostly check-ins and small repairs. She is independent.

follow_ups.question: Who helped with your mother?
follow_ups.response: Karen did the most, and I handled rides or house fixes when I could.

transcript.question_text: Tell me what it has been like trying to get the health care you or your immediate family need. Have you ever had to forgo getting the health care you need?
transcript.response: I have put off care, especially dental and physical therapy. When you are self-employed or subcontracting, insurance can be thin and time off costs money twice. I go if something seems serious, but I have let aches ride longer than I should. The clinic is decent, but appointments can be weeks out.

follow_ups.question: What care did you delay most recently?
follow_ups.response: A dental crown. I patched along until it hurt enough to deal with.

follow_ups.question: What makes care easier?
follow_ups.response: Clear pricing and appointments outside work hours.

transcript.question_text: Have you or your immediate family ever used alternative forms of medicine? This might include indigenous, non-western, or informal forms of care.
transcript.response: Nothing too far out. I have used massage, stretching, ice baths after surfing, and herbal teas my neighbor swears by. My mom used to rub Vicks on everything, like a lot of families. I believe doctors first, but I do not mind practical home remedies if they are not replacing real care.

follow_ups.question: Have you tried acupuncture or chiropractic care?
follow_ups.response: I tried a chiropractor once for my back. It helped a little, but I did not keep going.

follow_ups.question: Do you use herbs from your garden?
follow_ups.response: Rosemary and lavender mostly for cooking or smell, not medicine.

transcript.question_text: During tough times, some people tell us they cope by smoking or drinking. How about for you?
transcript.response: I do not smoke cigarettes. I drink beer, mostly weekends or watching a game, and I have had periods after the divorce where I drank more than I should. These days I try to keep it to a couple beers, not every night. Surfing early helps because you do not want to paddle out feeling lousy.

follow_ups.question: What is a typical week for alcohol?
follow_ups.response: Maybe three or four beers total, more if there is a barbecue or playoff game.

follow_ups.question: What do you do instead when stressed?
follow_ups.response: Walk the beach, play guitar, or work on the car.

transcript.question_text: Other people say they cope by relying on prescriptions, pain medications, marijuana, or other substances. How about for you and can you describe your most recent experience of using them, if any?
transcript.response: I use over-the-counter ibuprofen for pain. I do not take prescription pain pills. I have used marijuana gummies a few times for sleep or soreness, legally bought, but not often because I do not like feeling foggy. Most recent was maybe two months ago after a hard week painting stair rails, half a gummy before bed.

follow_ups.question: Do you worry about dependence?
follow_ups.response: Yes, which is why I keep it limited. I have seen guys in trades get tangled up with pills.

follow_ups.question: Does marijuana help?
follow_ups.response: It helps sleep sometimes, but I would rather be tired than cloudy the next morning.

transcript.question_text: How are you and your family coping with, or paying for, your health care needs right now?
transcript.response: I pay monthly for a basic health plan and handle co-pays as they come. My kids have their own coverage through work or plans they found. I keep a little savings for medical surprises, but one serious thing could drain it. For routine stuff, I compare costs and sometimes use urgent care if I cannot get in.

follow_ups.question: Do medical bills affect your budget?
follow_ups.response: Yes. Dental bills especially get put on a card or paid in chunks.

follow_ups.question: Do you help your kids with health costs?
follow_ups.response: Not regularly, but I would if they were stuck.

transcript.question_text: Some people are excited about medical vaccination, and others, not so much. How about you?
transcript.response: I am generally for vaccines. I got the COVID shots and boosters when recommended, and I get a flu shot most years. I do ask questions, but I am not anti-vaccine.

follow_ups.question: Did you have concerns about COVID vaccination?
follow_ups.response: A little at first because it felt fast, but my doctor explained it.

follow_ups.question: Did work influence that?
follow_ups.response: Yes. I go into people's homes, so I wanted to lower risk.

transcript.question_text: What are your trusted sources of information about the vaccine?
transcript.response: My doctor first, then the county public health site, and sometimes pharmacy information. I do not trust random Facebook posts. Sarah also reads more than I do and will send me something from a hospital or CDC page if she thinks I should see it.

follow_ups.question: Do you watch TV news for health information?
follow_ups.response: A little local news, but I do not rely on cable panels.

follow_ups.question: Who in your circle is most skeptical?

transcript.response: It was a neighborhood grocery store. They sold food, household goods, deli items, meat, produce, all the regular grocery stuff. The deli made sandwiches, salads, party trays, and prepared foods.

follow_ups.question: Was it a chain store?
follow_ups.response: Yes, a local chain at the time.

follow_ups.question: Did you visit her there?
follow_ups.response: Yes, and she would tell me not to touch everything.

transcript.question_text: Did your dad work for pay for at least a year while you were growing up?
transcript.response: Yes, he worked for pay the whole time I was growing up.

follow_ups.question: Was he the main earner?
follow_ups.response: Yes, most years.

follow_ups.question: Did he work long hours?
follow_ups.response: Yes, especially when overtime was available.

transcript.question_text: What was his job? What kind of work did he do? What were his most important activities or duties?
transcript.response: He did building maintenance and construction repair. He fixed plumbing, patched walls, painted, repaired doors, handled basic electrical, and kept apartment buildings or small commercial places running. He was the guy they called when something broke.

follow_ups.question: Did he teach you tools?
follow_ups.response: Yes, mostly by making me hold the flashlight and then try things.

follow_ups.question: Was he patient?
follow_ups.response: Not always, but he knew his stuff.

transcript.question_text: What kind of place did he work for? What kind of business was it? What did they make or do where he worked?
transcript.response: He worked for property management companies and small contractors. They maintained apartment buildings, rental houses, and small commercial properties. They did repairs, turnovers, remodel fixes, and emergency maintenance.

follow_ups.question: Did that shape your trade path?
follow_ups.response: Definitely. I grew up around tools, paint, and repairs.

follow_ups.question: Did you ever work with him?
follow_ups.response: A few times when I was young, mostly cleanup and simple tasks.

transcript.question_text: We all have hopes about what our future will look like. Imagine yourself a few years from now. Maybe you want your life to be the same in some ways as it is now. Maybe you want it to be different in some ways. What do you hope for?
transcript.response: In a few years I hope I have my contractor license, GED finished, and a small green-building painting business running steady. I would like two apprentices, maybe younger people who need the same chance Ray gave me. I want to do less heavy ladder work and more estimating, color consulting, quality checks, and mentoring. Personally, I want to stay near the water, keep surfing, take Mateo fishing, and maybe finally make that trip to Hossegor in France if money allows. I do not need to be rich. I want stability, health, respect in my trade, and enough time to enjoy the coast I worked so hard to stay near.

follow_ups.question: What is the first step toward that future?
follow_ups.response: Finish GED prep and schedule the contractor license exam.

follow_ups.question: What do you want to keep unchanged?
follow_ups.response: My connection to the ocean, my family, and doing hands-on work well.

transcript.question_text: What do you value the most in your life?
transcript.response: Family, honest work, independence, and the ocean. I value being useful. If my kids can call me, if a client trusts my word, if a helper learns something from me, that matters. I also value quiet time because I spent a lot of life rushing. A clean wave, a good paint line, a grilled fish taco with family around the table, those are not fancy things, but they feel like a good life.

follow_ups.question: What value did your parents pass down strongest?
follow_ups.response: Self-reliance and doing the job right.

follow_ups.question: What value do you want Mateo to learn from you?
follow_ups.response: Respect your work, respect people, and do not be afraid to learn with your hands.
